content: Cefprozil demonstrates in vitro activity against a wide spectrum of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Its bactericidal effect is achieved through the inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis. Cefprozil has been proven effective against most strains of specific microorganisms in both in vitro studies and clinical infections, as outlined in the Indications and Usage section. Aerobic Gram-Positive Microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (including strains that produce β-lactamase). Note: Cefprozil is not effective against methicillin-resistant staphylococci (MRSA). Streptococcus pneumoniae. Streptococcus pyogenes. Aerobic Gram-Negative Microorganisms: Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Moraxella (Branhamella) catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Additional In Vitro Data: Cefprozil has demonstrated minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of ≤8 mcg/mL against most (≥90%) strains of the following microorganisms. However, the clinical relevance of these findings is uncertain, as the safety and efficacy of cefprozil in treating infections caused by these organisms have not been established in well-controlled clinical trials. Aerobic Gram-Positive Microorganisms: Enterococcus durans. Enterococcus faecalis. Listeria monocytogenes. Staphylococcus epidermidis. Staphylococcus saprophyticus. Staphylococcus warneri. Streptococcus agalactiae. Streptococci (Groups C, D, F, and G). Viridans group streptococci. Note: Cefprozil is not effective against Enterococcus faecium. Aerobic Gram-Negative Microorganisms: Citrobacter diversus. Escherichia coli. Klebsiella pneumoniae. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Proteus mirabilis. Salmonella species. Shigella species. Vibrio species. Note: Cefprozil is not effective against most strains of Acinetobacter, Enterobacter, Morganella morganii, Proteus vulgaris, Providencia, Pseudomonas, and Serratia. Anaerobic Microorganisms: Prevotella (Bacteroides) melaninogenicus. Clostridium difficile. Clostridium perfringens. Fusobacterium species. Peptostreptococcus species. Propionibacterium acnes. Note: Most strains of the Bacteroides fragilis group are resistant to cefprozil. Susceptibility Testing: Dilution Techniques: Quantitative methods are employed to determine the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of cefprozil, which estimate the susceptibility of bacteria to the drug. These MICs should be determined using standardized procedures, such as broth or agar dilution methods, with defined inoculum concentrations and cefprozil powder concentrations. The results are interpreted as follows: Susceptible: The pathogen is likely to be inhibited if the drug concentration in the blood reaches typical therapeutic levels. Intermediate: The result is equivocal, and further testing or alternative drugs may be required. This category may indicate potential efficacy in specific body sites where the drug concentrates or when higher doses are used. Resistant: The pathogen is unlikely to be inhibited at achievable drug concentrations, and alternative therapy should be considered. Specific MIC values for cefprozil should be achieved with these control strains. Diffusion Techniques: A standardized procedure involves the use of paper disks impregnated with 30 mcg of cefprozil. The results of the disk diffusion test are interpreted similarly to those of dilution techniques, correlating the zone diameter with the MIC. For quality control, the 30 mcg cefprozil disk should produce specific zone diameters in laboratory test strains.
